common_name: Big Momma Heuchera (Giant Fragrant Villosa Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; as a villosa selection it shrugs off summer heat and humidity far better than micrantha-type hybrids.

directions: Big Momma was introduced by Terra Nova Nurseries for its unusually large, intensely fragrant pink flower spikes, which rise well above the broad, crinkled, forest-green foliage typical of villosa-type coral bells. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving afternoon protection in hotter zones; the thick, heat-tolerant leaves resist the summer decline that afflicts micrantha-derived hybrids. The late-summer bloom period extends the coral bells season later than most cultivars, making it useful for pairing with fall-interest companions. Divide congested crowns every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom size.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil on a rock garden slope or scree in partial sun; this Rocky Mountain native resents the rich, moisture-retentive beds that suit eastern Heuchera species.

directions: Bracted alumroot is a compact rock-garden species native to limestone cliffs and talus slopes of the central Rocky Mountains from Colorado and Wyoming into Utah and New Mexico. Small clusters of cream to greenish-white bell flowers, each subtended by a distinctive leafy bract, rise on short wiry stems above tidy rounded leaves. Unlike the shade-woodland Heuchera species grown in eastern gardens, it demands sharp drainage and lean, mineral soil, thriving in crevice gardens and alpine troughs rather than humus-rich borders. Avoid summer overwatering, which quickly rots the crown in this drought-adapted montane species.

planting.note: Plant in a gravelly, sharply drained crevice or rock garden pocket in partial shade; this Sandia Mountains endemic needs cool roots and dry crowns, not rich garden soil.

directions: Sandia alumroot is a diminutive cushion-forming species endemic to rocky crevices and cliff ledges of the Sandia and Manzano Mountains near Albuquerque, New Mexico, prized by rock gardeners for its tight mound of small, rounded, deeply veined leaves. Tiny pink to coral bell-shaped flowers appear on short stems rarely exceeding six inches, well below the height of most garden coral bells. Because it evolved on exposed granite outcrops, it requires exceptionally sharp drainage and tolerates drought far better than wet feet, making it a natural fit for alpine troughs and crevice gardens rather than conventional shade beds. Protect it from prolonged summer humidity at low elevation, which it did not evolve to tolerate.
sources: New Mexico Rare Plants Technical Council

planting.note: Plant in rocky, fast-draining soil in partial sun to partial shade; this Great Basin native comes from arid desert mountain ranges and needs much less water than humid-climate Heuchera species.

directions: Pink alumroot occurs naturally on dry, rocky canyon walls and mountain outcrops across the Great Basin, from eastern California and Nevada into Utah and Arizona, and is valued by xeric rock gardeners for its drought tolerance. Loose sprays of small pink to rose-colored flowers rise above a low mound of rounded, scalloped leaves in late spring to early summer. Because it is adapted to a desert mountain climate with cold winters and bone-dry summers, it performs best in lean, mineral soil with excellent drainage rather than the humus-rich beds favored by eastern woodland Heuchera. Established plants need little supplemental water once rooted and resent heavy clay or poorly drained sites.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in partial sun; this Colorado endemic is a compact, cold-hardy rock garden species that has been used as a breeding parent for dwarf coral bells cultivars.

directions: Hall's alumroot is a small, tidy species native to rocky slopes and crevices of the southern Rocky Mountains in Colorado, where it forms a neat mound of rounded, lightly lobed leaves well under a foot tall. Slender stems carry sparse clusters of small cream to pale pink flowers in early summer, well above the compact foliage mass. Its naturally dwarf habit and cold hardiness have made it a useful parent species in breeding programs aimed at smaller, more refined coral bells cultivars. In the garden it is best suited to rock gardens, scree beds, or trough plantings with sharp drainage rather than conventional shaded perennial borders.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Pacific Northwest woodland native tolerates far more moisture and shade than the dryland Rocky Mountain Heuchera species.

directions: Green-flowered alumroot grows naturally in moist coniferous forests and along stream banks from British Columbia south through Washington and Oregon, favoring conditions far shadier and damper than most garden coral bells tolerate. Tall, slender flowering stems carry airy spikes of small greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers well above the rounded, lightly hairy basal leaves, attracting hummingbirds and native pollinators in open woodland settings. It suits naturalistic Pacific Northwest and woodland gardens better than formal borders, pairing well with ferns, trilliums, and other moisture-loving shade natives. Keep soil consistently moist and rich in leaf litter, since this species does not tolerate the dry, lean conditions preferred by desert-adapted Heuchera relatives.

planting.note: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally on a slope or rocky bank; this coastal-mountain species comes from seeping cliffs and talus and dislikes standing water as much as prolonged drought.

directions: Alpine alumroot grows on moist, shaded cliffs, talus slopes, and streambanks from Alaska down through the coastal and Cascade mountains of British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, and California. The glossy, smooth-surfaced, maple-like leaves distinguish it from the hairier foliage of most other Heuchera species, and small white to pinkish flowers appear in loose, airy sprays in early summer. It prefers cool root conditions and steady moisture without waterlogging, making it well suited to rock gardens with seepage or shaded stream-bank plantings rather than standard dry borders. Give it protection from hot afternoon sun, especially at lower elevations outside its cool native range.
